title: US companies are seeking fewer foreign developers, and more "AI engineers"
content:
US companies are seeking fewer foreign software developers, and far more “AI engineers”
Comparing October through June of each year, H-1B filings for software developers fell 36% from fiscal 2022 to fiscal 2026, while filings for jobs with AI or machine learning in the title tripled. Microsoft and Google cut their software filings sharply; Amazon and Nvidia filed more.
Before a US employer can sponsor a foreign worker for an H-1B, the main US work visa for skilled professionals such as software engineers, it must file a Labor Condition Application, or LCA, with the Department of Labor, attesting that it will pay at least the prevailing wage for the job. The department publishes each application it decides, including the job title the employer wrote, in its LCA disclosure data, about half a million certified H-1B filings a year. Together these filings form a public record of which roles companies want to fill with foreign workers and what companies call those roles. The federal fiscal year starts in October and the latest published data runs through June 2026, so we compare October through June of each fiscal year.
Software filings fell more than twice as fast as H-1B filings overall
- Software filings fell 36% from fiscal 2022 to fiscal 2026, comparing October through June of each year.
- Filings for new hires fell even faster. Counting only filings for new employment rather than renewals or employer changes, software fell 46%.
- Filings with AI job titles are still rare. They made up 1.8% of all certified H-1B filings in fiscal 2026.
Software filings fell in two steps. They dropped 27% in fiscal 2023, a year of widespread tech layoffs, and recovered slightly by 2025. They fell another 14% in fiscal 2026, most steeply from October to December 2025, right after the White House announced a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions. That quarter was down 26% from a year earlier; by April to June, the gap had narrowed to 5%.
Some of the growth in AI job titles may be existing work under a new name. Titles that spell out “machine learning” or “artificial intelligence” rose 80%, while shorter titles such as “AI engineer” grew much faster and supplied 92% of the latest year’s increase.
More than three times as many employers now use AI job titles
- Most employers filed just one. Two-thirds of fiscal 2026’s employers with AI job titles submitted a single filing.
- The biggest filers’ share is shrinking. Employers outside the five largest submitted 85% of AI-titled filings in fiscal 2026, up from 75%.
- Growth doesn’t depend on the biggest filers. Leaving out fiscal 2026’s five largest, among them Apple, LinkedIn and Meta, AI-titled filings still rose 250%.
OpenAI and Anthropic rarely put AI in their job titles. Of their 402 certified filings from October through June of fiscal 2026, only 11% included AI or machine learning in the title; most were for some version of “Member of Technical Staff.”
Software filings rose at some of the largest tech firms and fell sharply at others
- Microsoft’s software filings fell 44% and Google’s 33%, two of the three steepest drops among the nine companies, along with Salesforce’s.
- Nvidia’s nearly quadrupled and Amazon’s rose 34%. Amazon’s share of all software filings rose to 8.8% from 4.2%.
- The decline is concentrated outside big tech. The nine companies combined filed 6% fewer for software developers; all other employers filed 41% fewer.
How we built this
We used the Department of Labor’s quarterly LCA disclosure files from fiscal 2022 through the third quarter of fiscal 2026, counting each certified H-1B filing once and dating it by its decision. Software developers are filings in the software-developer occupation codes, minus those with AI job titles so the two groups don’t overlap; including them, software still fell 34%. AI job titles contain “machine learning”, “artificial intelligence”, “AI” or “ML” as whole words. Employers are counted by legal name, and company families group the legal names that begin with each company’s name.
An LCA is an employer’s attestation filed before a visa petition. It isn’t an approved visa, a hire or a unique worker, and one filing can cover several positions or a renewal for someone already employed; counting requested positions instead of filings, software fell 25%. Employers write their own job titles, which can change without any change in the work, and these counts can’t show whether AI caused any of the shift.

report.summary: H-1B filings for software developers fell 36% from fiscal 2022 to fiscal 2026, while AI-titled roles tripled as US employers rebrand hiring around AI engineers.
report.background: The H-1B is the main US work visa for skilled professionals, and before sponsoring one an employer must file a Labor Condition Application (LCA) with the Department of Labor, disclosing the job title it intends to use. Those roughly half a million certified filings a year form a public, quarterly record of which roles companies want to fill with foreign workers and what they call them. The new analysis compares October-through-June windows across fiscal years 2022 to 2026. The shift unfolded against mass tech layoffs in 2023, a generative-AI hiring boom, and a White House announcement of a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions, which landed just as software filings dropped again. Crucially, employers write their own titles, so the data captures labeling as well as genuine demand.
key_points: Software developer filings fell 36% between fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2026, and 46% when counting only new hires rather than renewals or transfers. That is more than twice the overall decline in H-1B filings. AI-titled filings tripled over the same period, but still made up just 1.8% of all certified filings, so the two trends are nowhere near offsetting each other.

The software drop came in two steps: a 27% fall in fiscal 2023 during widespread tech layoffs, a slight recovery by 2025, then another 14% decline in fiscal 2026. The steepest quarter was October to December 2025, down 26% year over year, right after the $100,000 H-1B fee was announced; by April to June the gap had narrowed to 5%.

Much of the AI growth looks like relabeling. Titles spelling out machine learning or artificial intelligence rose 80%, but short titles like AI engineer grew far faster and supplied 92% of the latest year's increase. Three times as many employers now use AI job titles, and two-thirds of them filed just one, suggesting scattered rebranding rather than a concentrated hiring surge.

Big tech diverged sharply. Microsoft's software filings fell 44% and Google's 33%, among the steepest drops; Nvidia's nearly quadrupled and Amazon's rose 34%, lifting Amazon's share of all software filings from 4.2% to 8.8%. The nine largest filers collectively cut software filings only 6%, while everyone else cut 41%, so the decline is concentrated outside big tech.

AI-native labs barely use AI in titles. Of OpenAI's and Anthropic's 402 certified filings from October to June of fiscal 2026, only 11% mentioned AI or machine learning; most were for some version of Member of Technical Staff, a reminder that job titles are unreliable proxies for what engineers actually work on.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the data suggests the talent shift is smaller and more cosmetic than headline numbers imply: AI-titled roles are growing fast from a tiny base, and a large share of the movement is employers renaming existing work rather than creating net-new AI positions. The $100,000 fee appears to have suppressed new petitions quickly, then partly faded, meaning immigration policy is now a live variable in AI hiring capacity. For developers, especially foreign nationals, the visa route into US software roles is narrowing while AI-flavored titles and startups outside big tech absorb some of the slack, pushing more engineers toward AI skills and toward employers willing to sponsor. For regular users, the practical effect is indirect: less global competition for conventional software roles may ease wage pressure, but a relabeling-heavy labor market makes it harder to judge whether products are genuinely AI-driven or just renamed.
report.tools: To follow the underlying data, explore the Department of Labor's quarterly LCA disclosure files, the USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub, and sites like h1bdata.info and MyVisaJobs for employer-level filing histories. Analysts can reproduce this kind of study with DuckDB or pandas over the raw LCA CSVs, and h1bdata-style open-source parsers on GitHub help normalize the files. For job seekers, watching title conventions on LinkedIn and levels.fyi helps distinguish genuine AI roles from rebranded ones.
